brief.topic: The Sequence Missing from Every Infinite List

s01: Imagine a list of every infinite sequence of zeros and ones.
Each row continues forever. The rows are numbered one, two, three, and so on.
We can build a sequence that this list misses.
Read the first digit of row one, and flip it.
Read the second digit of row two, and flip that.
Continue diagonally, changing zero to one and one to zero.
The new sequence differs from row one at its first digit.
It differs from row two at its second digit.
For any numbered row, it differs at that row number. So it cannot equal any row in the list.
Only a finite corner fits on this screen. The argument applies to every positive row number.
There is no list indexed by the natural numbers containing all infinite binary sequences. This is uncountability.
What if we add the missing sequence to a new list?
Apply the same diagonal construction to that new list. It misses a different sequence.
The obstacle is not a bad ordering. Every proposed complete list can be defeated.

scenes.narration:
Imagine a list of every infinite sequence of zeros and ones. Each row continues forever. The rows are numbered one, two, three, and so on.

We can build a sequence that this list misses. Read the first digit of row one, and flip it. Read the second digit of row two, and flip that. Continue diagonally, changing zero to one and one to zero.

The new sequence differs from row one at its first digit. It differs from row two at its second digit. For any numbered row, it differs at that row number. So it cannot equal any row in the list.

Only a finite corner fits on this screen. The argument applies to every positive row number. There is no list indexed by the natural numbers containing all infinite binary sequences. This is uncountability.

What if we add the missing sequence to a new list? Apply the same diagonal construction to that new list. It misses a different sequence. The obstacle is not a bad ordering. Every proposed complete list can be defeated.
